VARIE TIES. An Awkward Predicament. þÿ Several rival manufacturers of articles in India rubber have lately figured in more than one of our Courts of Law, contending for the exclusive privilege of manufacturing articles of apparel, in which this glutinous substance has recently been introduced. If the following story prove true, its consumption may not prove altogether so extensive as is contemplated. A party lately went out from Boston (United States) on a fishing excursion ; and, in order to secure themselves against all danger of being drenched either bv rain or spray, they were provided with India rubber garments, said to be waterproof While enjoying themselves over their wine, a toast was given, which it was proposed should be received with all due honours. Accordingly bumpers were filled, and, with glass in hand, every one essayed to rise þÿ but in vain, luckless mortals that they were ! an indissoluble connection had been formed between the indispensable part of their nether garments and the chairs. An unliquidated bond had been entered into : and it was found utterly impossible to raise the gentlemen from their silting posture without the aid of a tackle. We suppose that some of the sea deities were at the bottom of this piece of enchantment, revenge for the intrusion into their domains made by these piscatory depredators. þÿ American Paper.

The Comet has been visible for the last three nights, but with no brilliancy, having merely the appearance of a dim misty star somewhat enlarged. Its nearest approach to the earth was on Monday last, and it is calculated that it will now pass rapidly to the South, so that no apprehension need be entertained of any danger to our planet from this wandering visitor. The only thing remarkable about it is the extreme accuracy of the calculations respecting the time of its approach, and the path of its course. When we first observed it on Saturday night, at nine o'clock, it was immediately above the pointers of the Great Bear, or, which will be as instructive to most of onr readers, above the " stilts of the Plough and last night hefore eight o'clock it rose immediately above the two stars farther South, which, with the pointers, form a sort of square. It is approaching the next star in that Constellation, Alioth, commonly called the first star in the tail of the Great Bear.

Tiie Navigation of tiie Delaware. þÿ The immense amount of property now on board of vessels in the Delaware, between Newcastle and the Breakwater, has naturally, says the Philadelphia Gazette, excited the solicitude of the merchants. A number of ships with cargoes, worth in the aggregate, perhaps several millions of dollars, are now lying without adequate protection against the ice, which must break up in a few days before the city. þÿ The ice-boat is preparing to attempt to cut her way down to Newcastle, in order to be at hand to render assistance, should it be needed ; and it is not improbable, that owing to the want of piers at that place, to afford a shelter for vessels drawing much water, some of thein will be obliged to return to the Breakwater, after having approached within forty iniles of Philadelphia.

Washington, March 7, 1830 þÿ From Annapolis we learn that His Britannic Majesty's brig Wanderer, Capt. Dclbo, arrived at that port on Thursday last, and on Friday landed Air. Fox, who succeeds Sir C. It. \ uughan as Alinister Plenipotentiary and Envoy Extraordinary from Great Britain to the United States. Mr Fox was received with the usual hospitality of the capital of Maryland, and has accepted of a public, ball, given to him and the officers of the British Government vessel, lie will probably reach this city to-morrow or the next day. The Baltimore Chronicle remarks: þÿ The arrival at Annapolis of the Hon. Air. Fox, the New British Minister, has been in. proved by the citizens of that ancient Capital, in a manner worthy of its renown for elegant hospitality. He has been invited to and has accepted a ball which took place yesterday evening, and which doubtless attracted all the fashion and beauty of Annapolis and its vicinity. This manifestation of the sense entertained by our fellow citizens of the kind and fraternal oiler of Great Britain to mediate between France and the United States, cannot fail to be gratifying to Mr. Fox and to the Government he represents. It is evident, that there is, in every part of Great Britain, a strong inclination to cultivate the best feelings towards the United States. The late magnanimous effort to prevent a rupture with France is the most conspicuous evidence of this disposition, but an incident which is related in the papers, and which we
w ill here recount, shows that it is not confined to the members of the Government.

Texas. þÿ The arrival in this city of Scnor Gokostiza, Envoy Extraordinai y and Minister Plenipotentiary from the Republic of Mexico, (as it is still called,) has produced no inconsiderable excitement among those who have taken an interest in the affairs of Texas; and as it is admitted by the Envoy and his suite, that this is a special mission which will not in any way interfere w ith the resident minister, it is very generally supposed that it relates directly to Texas, and the struggle which that province is so nobly sustaining against the Despotic sway ol Santa Anna. This supposition is increased by the annunciation in a Government paper at I era Cruz, that this mission is one ol a high confidential character and involving grave public considerations. The impression among the best informed seems to be, and we incline to the same opinion, that the impoverished state of the Mexican Treasury, added to the unsettled state of Santa Anna's Government and the evident determination of Texians not to submit to it, have at length induced the authori ties of Mexico to enter into the discussion of the subject of boundary between that country and the United States. We know that the representatives from this country to Alexico, have repeatedly been instructed to impress upon the Mexican authorities that instead of adopting an im. ciliary line somewhere in the vicinity of the Nueces, the heart of Texas, to which we have laid claim, it is the interests of both Governments, that our jurisdiction

should be at once extended to the great desert which reaches to within sixty miles south of the Riu (j ramie, and which is a natural boundary between the two countries. This desert, upon which nothing but the l'riekley Pear grows, and which is as barren, and almost as impassable as that of Sahara would forever be a barrier between the two countries, which could not fail to prevent those disscnlions and border disturbances, always the consequent ; of a mere imaginary boundary or some si .ail river, and which in future time would necessarily lead to wars with all their attendant evils. I he correctness of this view is so obvious to every observer of tne least reflection, that there can be no doubt Mexico has long felt it truth. Slape. þÿ During the recent visit of the Princess Victoria to Wentworth House, much of the time of the royal party was occupied in perambulating the beautiful grounds adjoining that mansion. On one of these occasions, her Royal Highness, being in advance ol the party, was respectfully cautioned by an under gardener, not to take a certain waik, as the late rain had made the ground in a particular situation in it, " slape " " Slape, stupe," said the Princess, with the characteristic inquisitiveness of a descendant ol George 111., "and pray what is slape?" "Very slippy, Madam," replied the man. However in spite of the warning thus given, like a genuine sprig of the House of Brunswick, onward she gaily proceeded. On reaching the " slape" ground, down she came. " i here," shouted the noble owner ot the grounds, who, on perceiving no injury was done, laughingly approached, þÿ " Now your Royal Highness has received an explanation of the term 'slape,' both theoretically and practically." "Yes," rejoined the good humoured Princess, " I shall never forget the meaning of slape.'" 0 0 Petticoat Government. þÿ The aspect of European affairs promises realize, in three to principal kingdoms within the present century, all the dreaded horrors of that bugbear of domestic life þÿ petticoat government ! Already in Portugal and Spain, are two Queens Regent, and in this country a Queen rises in the ascendant of the future. The present Queen of Portugal, and the expectant Queen of En-

gland are of an age þÿ the former having been born in April, 1819, the latter in May, 1819, each being therefore, in her seventeenth year. The Queen of Spain, Donna Isabella, was bom 10th of October, 1830, and is, therefore, only in her fifth þÿyear. But looking at the ages of the parties, there is reason to believe that they will, in full maturity of power sway the destinies of their respective nations concurrently for many years þÿ a royal sisterhood ! Byron, as devoted a worshipper ol the petticoats as was Ferdinand himself, says, " Smite woman. and die world is wualr before thee!"

Extraordinary Swindling. A man dressed in shabby clothing applied a few days ago to a gentleman named Potts, residing Sandymount, for his signature to a in paper, purporting to be a mendicant petition. Mr. Potts, without a very close examination of the document, unhesitatingly signed it at the solicitation of the individual. He was not, however, a little confounded on learning, some time after, that his order for £400 had been duly honoured at the bank of Messrs. La Touche, where he had a considerable sum of money lodged. It turned out that the so called petition had been ingeniously placed over the order in question, and had been removed previously to its presentation at the bank. þÿ The delinquent, whose person was completely unknown to Mr. Potts, has not since been hoard þÿol. His Excellency the Governor-General gave a brilliant Ball arid Supper at the Government House on Friday evening, to the numerous American Ladies and Gentlemen, who have visited our island the present season, in pursuit of health, and most of whom arc now about leaving us. þÿ The Supper Tables were elegantly decorated and sumptuously spread and the American and ! > Flags in Union, were tastefully displayed upon them. A brilliant dis> of the fashion and beauty of the Island graced the Pall loom. þÿ The Dancing commenced at ; early hour, and was only suspended at J 2 o'clock, by His Excellency taking the lead into the Supper room, and handing a venerable American lady to her seat at the tables ; at v\,.ich about three hundred guests ; artcok of the munilicem hospitality ol the Governor General. " Our ft lends of the United Stat After Supper fits Excellency gave tne toast ," which was responded to by one of the American Gentlemen, who proposed in return " The Government of St. Croix, liberal in its principles and paternal in its character."þÿ The health of .lis Excellency ' Governor General von Scholten," upon his retiring to the Bail room, was drank in bumpers of Champaigne accompanied with " three times three" hearty cheers Abundance of this exhilirating wine was served to all the company. The dancing was again resumed after Supper, and continued to a late hour, when the company retired, pleased and gratified with their hospitable reception, and with the urbanity dis-
played by His Excellency towards bis American guests, and to all present.

Thirty and forty years ago, you could not pass through Hoiborn, during a certain portion of the year, without observing a siring of carriages drawn up near a large house, the upper floors of which appealed magnilicently furnished ; and the groups of well-dressed people seen going in and coining out, could not, if you had a grain of Eve's curse in your composition, but make you ask who it was that received so many lashionable visiters in such a dingy district. You were informed that the celebrated Mrs. Williams, the renowned caster of nativities and teller of fortunes, honored Holborn by residing in it : and it you were fortunate enough to meet amongst your male friends one who had patU die lady a visit, you heard that she was a very handsome, though somewhat dark woman. The females differed on the subject of her beauty, influenced doubtless by the good or ill fortune foretold to them. Amongst the numerous applicants to this Lilly in petticoats, site had the honor of numbering the Prince of Wales : and although Ins lvoyal Highness endeavored to preserve a strict incognito, he was hailed by his tide on entering the abode of astrological lesearch.þÿ The Prince did not scruple to tell the result of his visit. " The lady informs me that I shall live to be King, although my stars decree i am not to be crowned." In the autumn Mrs Williams usually visited the various resorts of fashion, Rath, Clifton, liotwells, Brighton, &c., and it was during her sojourn at the two former places tiiat

what 1 am about to relate occurred. No sooner was her arrival known in the city of Bladud, titan her doors were besieged by persons of all classes ; as it had been duly announced that a simple consultation was within the reach of the humblest, whilst an examination of the heavenly bodies, to ascertain whethor or not your star was on the dennes om Eftermiddagen Kl : 1 slet : þÿ ascendant, must be remunerated by a price too exorbitant for the superstitious in the middle walks of life. Amongst the first who found themselves confronted with this awlul personage were Flan, Overslag og Conditioner- two young ladies of family : the largest douceur was tendered ; and our Cassandra commenced turning over the leaves of a mystic volume. Suddenly the book was closed, and she started abruptly from her chair. Then, leading one of the girls aside, she said impressively to her, " 1 am too ill to take any trouble for that poor dear child to-day ; you must leave rnc now, but only on this condition, that you," and she grasped the hand of her auditor, whilst her dark eyes seemed almost lit up by supernatural lire, " you must solemnly pro-

dtnatAMsruaA mise to come to me to-morrow, let what will have chanced. "Pis well þÿ now go !" Faithful to her word, the terrified girl returned the next day ; " I ask not for your companion of yesterday," exclaimed Mrs. Williams, " she is dead !" A burst of tears from her afflicted friend conlirmed the fatal sentence. This fearful tale was speedily told; and hundreds flocked to look upon and consult the same mysterious oracle. The late countess of M conceived it possible, by a simple artifice, to puzzle the conjurer, and accordingly attired herself in humble garb, taking with her the well dressed governess, on whose finger her Ladyship had placed her own wedding ring. A guinea was tendered by Miss , whilst her mistress, trying to assume a rusticity of manner, dropped curtesy, a and offered a crown piece þÿ Their separate palms were scrutinized by Mrs. W., who, after a brief investigation, turned to the matron, saying, " Why do you suffer that woman to wear your ring ? is it not enougli that she has already usurped your rights? þÿ aye, blush and tiemble, girl." Mrs. W. was right. An elderly maiden had lost many articles of plate, jewellery, and wearing apparel. þÿ Their unaccountable disappearance had caused the most serious uneasiness to her housekeeper, a trusty creature, who never left her home except on a Sunday evening to attend Lady Huntingdon's chapel, but whose stay-athome habits were broken thro' by the sudden determination of her lady to visit Mrs. Williams, in the hope of obtaining some informa-

tion respecting the missing property. The pious domestic talked about tampering with Satan Saul, and the Witch of Endor, in vain. Miss F had made up her mind to go, and what was more, to take her trusty Sally with her as spokeswoman on the occasion ; the excellent spinster being of a nervous and timid temperament. They reached the dwelling of the Sj L»il ; Sally gave the fee and a list of the lost articles, adding þÿ " We shall be happy to pay you twice as much if you will assist us in finding them." " We and us, woman!" said Mrs, \\ iiliams, " I wonder how you ventured to come to me then turning to the alarmed mistress, she continued, " there stands the thief ! Down dropt Sally on her knees, confessed the fact, and, in consequence of her information, the house of the pewopener of her favorite chapel was searched, and the property found and restored.

The Merchant trades to foreign lands, And braves the billowy main ; And buys and sells, and schemes and plans. With views of future gain : But whelming waves, or wasting fire, May take his goods away ; Uncertain wealth I ne'er desire, Let me be rich to day.

The student, emulous of fame, Pursues the distant prize ; Be mine e'en now an honoured name, Acknowiedg'd by the wise. The lover too dreams of delight, His fondness to repay ; But ne'er let me the allection slight, Which crowns my love to day.

While others life incautious spend In wishing to reform ; Tomorrow to be good intend, But think not to perform ; A better purpose shall be mine, For danger waits delay ; But Heaven will on the morrow shine. If virtuous prove to day.
Resplendent orb ! bright sun 1 Who lend'st thy friendly aid to govern time With steady round þÿ thy glorious course is run And now thou shin'st anew o'er every clime.
The year is fled and gone ! With rapid flight it wing'd its short career. And this succeeding, this just entered on v Alike will pass as visionary air.
Each day, each fleeting hour, Brings jaack to man one dire uncertainty, As when was giv'n his breath by that greaf power, Which subjects ail on earth to fate's decree.
If time at length must cease, Why turn our eye from virtues sacred way? Or why prefer a life of slothful ease, And leave neglected each important day ?
If man is born to die. If one short moment may decide his doom. Let us improve the moments as they fly, Nor yet delay for days that ne'ei may come.
How wretched is the man, WI10 bows enslaved to fortunes baleful shrine Vain is his toil, and false his fav'rite plan. Scathing the soul when all his joys decline.
Charmed by some fatal spell, To blindly prosecute thy mad career, Fire the pale eve of life thy woes reveal, Unbend thy mind dispel thy guilty fear.
The choicest gifts of heav'n, Richly descending to increase thy store, With all thy other blessing daily given. Will haply tend thy future bliss to ensure

The increasing solicitude of the French Government to terminate amicably the differences that have arisen with the United States continues to be manifested, by articles in tire Ministerial Journals. The Monitcur of Thursday contains an article (adopted from the Journal de Paris) denying that the American Government had, directly or indirectly, announced to the Cabinet of the Tuilcrics that it was the intention of that Government to propose to Congress a Non-intercourse Act, and that it was equally false that the Government of France had indicated to that of the United States that, in sucli case, the former would declare war against the latter. The article in question proceeds to state that the warlike preparations of France are merely precautionary, and fully warranted, if not demanded, by the terms of the President's Message of last year. The Government of France was ready to fulfil the obligation imposed on it by the national honour and the law of 17th June last, and had only directed measures to enable it to repel an aggression, which neither by its words nor its actions would it nevertheless provoke. We shall only observe that this disclamor bears the mark of more haste and of more heat than its antecedents, and that it is a little of the latest to order preparations in November in consequence of certain passages in a discourse pronounced (or in a document published) in December last To speak of conciliation nuri ihe law" of the 17th June 1835, is an absurdity þÿ that law being saddled with

an amendment requiring explanations, and even satisfactions, which it is notorious the present Chief of the American Government will not give. How the parties will or can be led to approximate amicably, we shall not predict ? but notwithstanding the preparations of France for war, we have too much reliance on the peace-at-any price disposition of King Louis Philip, and upon the good sense of the Americau Legislature, to deem war inevitable. Although this is our own \icw of this extraordinary subject, we feel bound to state that the maratime preparations of France are pushed at this moment with an activity strongly contrasted with the indifference of the French Government up to this time, and which naturally suggests its apprehensions that the Message or the Prcsidant of the United States, now on its way to Europe, will have called for these precautionary measures. JD&STSR ( From the Philadelphia Gazette, Jan. 12.) THE FRENCH QUESTION STATED IN PLAIN ENGLISH. From the New York Star. France and the United States. Our friend of the Courier and Enquirer is very like General Jackson þÿ we beg pardon his for the comparison þÿ but he resembles his great prototype in being always ready square to off for a fight and always grumbling at those who decline falling in. From the first moment that a difficulty or difference of opinion appeared on the French question, he began to smell gunpowder, and he has continued to snuff it up ever since : and the last news from France has run him up to fever heat, and he beats the tattoo on the drum with immense fierceness, and although he intends to serve out the General after the fight, still he is not only willing himself to enlist under his banner, but has seized Daniel Webster by the arm, and is determined to get him at least in the thickest of the fight, which, if he succeeds in doing, then have, we mistaken the man." " The error in which the editor has fallen, is, supposing from the first jump ' that this is a question of national honor," instead of a " mere question of dollars and cents þÿ a debt acknowledged to be due, and which will in due time, we hope and trust, be paid. Let us strip this question of ambiguous covering and diplomatic phrases, and give the story in a language that every loco foco man in the country can understand. France agreed to pay us five millions by treaty but the chambers refused to ratify it þÿ The President in effect saj s, in his message

of 1834: þÿ "The blackguards are humming us : they intend to chest its ; their King is a knave þÿ there's no honor or good faith hi riim þÿ let's thrash him into compliance þÿ send out our privateers and capture his ships." The French Government, pursuing the same train of thought and language in return, says : l)iahle I attack our honor ? þÿ insult our Kiri" 1 þÿ charge us with swindling? þÿ declare war against us! O ho! General Jackson; money we owe you, money we intend to pay you, but you must explain away this offensive menace, silvous plait." ' I'll see you d d first," says old Hickory : I'll explain notli- " ing pay þÿ the money, or I'll lick you." Very " well," says Monsieur ; " If we are to be thrashed in this business, we must be prepared to receive the chastisement with all due grace." Now, where is the National Honor" in " all this affair? Why are the people to be called upon to sustain the rashness and folly of the President ? Why is war, with all its horrors, and with an old ally, to be stirred up for an affair, the whole of which is in the compass of a nut shell ? If our President had come from Down East, he would have managed to have got the money and preserved peace, without any sacrifice of the national honor, as it is called ; but General Jackson, from the moment lie acquired power, began to growl and grumble at all Europe, and to cast fierce glances at several of the South American Republics. Wherever we had a claim, just or equivocal, he made a direct dash

at it, and got from their fears what probably their sense of justice would not have allowed, lie intended to let the world know, that although ele cted the peaceable Chief Magistrate, of tins Republic, ho had not put off, entirely, his fighting propensities, and, therefore, thev had the alternative; the money or the ultima ratio: "a word and a blow," and the blow likely to come first; and, what not a

uaoawNNTOS AT'JSL little astonished foreign powers, he treated his own people with as little ceremony ; seized the public treasure þÿ kicked the Constitution out of doors, and proclaimed that he was the Government. He fed bis party and their retainers, with the silver spoon of patronage, until they rolled into the gutter of submission, and the intelligence and integrity ol the country were not strong enough to overcome this corruption. Justice may sometimes be procured at too dear a price ; and although this belligerent attitude has had the effect of bringing some of the smaller powers to terms, the manner of enforcing our claims on foreign nations, adopted by General Jackson, is calculated to make us enemies every where, and has had immense influence on France in preparing to resist such a course. The Courier &. Enquirer, in the fame strain, calls for non-intercourse þÿ calls for immediate action þÿ and speaks of a hostile fleet at our doors France no longer looks to General Jackson they look to Congress and þÿ we believe, that looking in that direction we are safe. No act of non-intercourse, or any act calculated to widen the breach, will, we are quite sure, be sanctioned by the Senate. All the preparations that should be made, will be made. The nation must be placed in an attitude of defence : our fortifications and ships must be manned. We must not be caught unprepared for a conflict if it cannot be avoided ; but we must not seek it. li the President provokes it, Congress must prove to the world that the President is not the Go-

vernment, and we are not responsible for bis acts A short time will place us in possession of the views of the French King, on the receipt of the last Message, which wc continue to hope and believe, will be satisfactory. Until then, no action, of any kind, on the treaty, is required.

LOSS OF ANOTHER CONVICT SHIP AND 220 LIVES. Van þÿDieman sI, and Papers to the 4th of July are received. They contain a most distressing and painful account of the wreck of another convict ship, with a still greater loss of life than in the case of the George the Third, only a few weeks before. The case is that of the female convict ship Neva, Captain Peek, which sailed from Cork on the 8th of January, having on board 150 female prisoners, with 83 of their children, nine free women, with 22 children, and a crew of 20, making in all 241 persons, including Dr. Stevenson, the Superintendant. Out of the whole number, only fifteen persons have survived the shipwreck ; namely, six of the female prisoners and nine of the crew. 1 he immediate cause of the wreck was a miscalculation of their dead reckoning, by which they ought to have been upwards of ninety miles from land, when they struck upon a reef on the coast of þÿKing Island s called Harbinger's Reef, near the entrance of Ross's Straits. The rudder was unshipped by the first shock, and the vessel thereby becoming unmanageable, she swung round on the rocks and immediately bilged. The boasts were instantly lowered, but all bilged as soon as they reached the water, and in a few minutes the ship separated in four divisions, those that were saved having been carried ashore on pieces of the floating wreck They were soon afterwards discovered by a small vessel belonging to Launceston, and carried into that port, where they were treated with great humanity. From the short time the vessel

held together after she struck, it is naturally inferred that she was defective in her timbers, and ought therefore not to have been employed in such a service, where so many lives were at stake. It is indeed further asserted that this is not a solitary case, hut that generally for several years past, sufficient attention has not been paid to the character of the ships employed to transport convicts to the colony. þÿ Naval and Military Gazette. 0 0 A Mob Patriot. þÿ When John Wilkes was rallied by the King for his apparent indifference to the cause of liberty, he coolly answered that he could assure Ids .Majesty, he never had been a Wilkite.

Extract from the Experiences of Surgeon, a in the Monthly Magazine. THE DEATH BED.

I had never yet seen the agonies of a deathbed, though the sight of human suffering was become familiar, and had ceased to excite those painful sensations which it had first created. I had seduloush avoided remaining to be a witness of the last struggles of mortality. went up stairs accompanied by the þÿhusband. On approaching the bedside, 1 was shocked perceive to that his wife was dying, and that all human aid was fruitless. She was a young, and must have been

a strikingly handsome woman ; but her fine features now bore the impress iof the destroyer. Her cheeks were sunk, hex nostrils and lips quivered during the respiration, a cold clammy sweat stood upon her forehead, and her countenance pinched, and wore that peculiar appearance, termed by us þÿ facies þÿhippocratica. I sat down ; her pulse was feeble and intermittent. She was slightly delirious ; but when roused, answered faintly and rationally. I enquired how she was, and if she suffered much ? þÿ þÿNo, she said, no, þÿ none whatever, it is quite gone. I am quite better ; and, when I have slept, shall be þÿwell. This was said slowly, and at intervals, and with imperfect articulation þÿ Her sister, who was in the room, and in high spirits, as the pain had left her, little imagining it was a fatal system, told me that for several days she had been in great agony. I called the husband aside, and shortly, but distinctly informed him that a very brief period, and his wife would be no more. He was startled, but incredulous ; þÿ she was easier, she must be better þÿ the doctor had told him so ; I shook my head, and desired him to go for her mother, who had just left the house, in the confident hope that her daughter was recovering. He obeyed me very reluctantly : and I again set down at the bed-side, waiting for his return, in order to summon the surgeon. The angel of death was, however, nearer than I imagined. A fitful and unmeaning smile played over her features ; her hands wandered about as if in

search of something : while the intervals between respiration became longer and longer ; her chest heaved, and that peculiar gurgling sound in the throat, known as the þÿ death þÿrattle, apprised me that the moment of dissolution was at hand. Her sister, terrified at these portentous changes, looking at me for information. I could only say, that in a few minutes all would be over. She fled shrieking out of the room, and I was left alone Some Wearing Apparel and Lin- j with the dying woman I sat gazing upon nen, a Silver Watch, a Mahoga- ! her, with a feeling of awe and dread ; I almost expected to see the dark form of Azarael stoop over his victim and the disembodied spirit wing its way from its earthly tabernacle. Beyond the picturing of my disturbed imagination there was nothing frightful ; no struggling as if mortality was freeing itself from its shackles of dust ; no distortion of lip or limb, as if the separation was a painful one : on the contrary, she lay perfectly still, Weigh- flitted the over and same bland, though unearthly smile her face ; and though her lips moved, the motion resembled those seen on the lips of childhood in its happy dreams. þÿ Not a sound broke the still silence of the apartment, save the rush of the fragrant breeze through the window, the slight rustle of the bed cloths made by the movements of her hands, and the low and occasional gurgling in her throat. My presence seemed, to my cowed and overawed mind, as something improper, so strongly was 1 impressed with the

conviction that þÿ a winded spirit was about to depart to its þÿhome. I gazed upon her with a species of fascination, without having power to withdraw my eyes n moment from her face, till at length, after a slight convulsive shudder, her eyelids were elevated and a deeper respiration took place. I waited in vain for its return. Her lower jaw fell, her arms and body lost their life like position þÿ she was dead. Buried in e.ontemplation, I remained motionless till I was roused by the hasty entrance of her husband mother and sieteft. Twenty

minutes past, and they had fondly believed her convalescent ; and they now found her a corpse. 1 withdrew to the window, and whilst a burst of passionate sorrow overpowered the mourners, they knelt round the bed, the heavy sobs of tbe man mingling with the wilder grief of the female 1 looked at the group ; what a contrast between the living and the dead ! She lay before them as if in a profound and heavy sleep, her features perceptibly changing and assuming smile beauty of expression, as the their original that had played over them was gradually waning, and as the muscles lost their irritability ; whilst they were weeping in all the attitudes of a first affliction, wringing their hands, and addressing her with vehement words of endearment. After these occurrences, it was my lot to see death in various shapes, from the calm preparation, the hope and confidence oi unshrinking innocence, to the frantic terror and fierce impenitence for guilt and materialism. By a beautiful and beneficent dispensation of Providence, it, however, but rarely happened that patients were at all conscious of the immediate approach ol dissolution: and 1 am not aware that in any instance which came under my personal notice, any sign was exhibited that the moment of extinction was anticipated. If I judge from what I have seen death, its pangs arc not painful, of and, consequently, the sense of it is most in apprehension.

A MAN AND TIGER COMBAT. (From the. Oriental Annual.) The next scene was of a far more awful character. A man entered the arena armed only with a Coorg knite. and clothed in short trousers, which barely covered his hips, and extended hall way4down the thighs. The instrument which he wielded in his right hand was a heavy blade, something like the coulter of a plough, about two feet long, and full three inches wide, gradually diminishing towards the handle, with which it iormed a right angle. This knife is used with great dexterity by the Coorgs ; being swung round in the hand before the blow is inflicted, and then brought into contact with the object intended to he struck with a force and effect truly astounding. The champion who now presented himself before the Rajah was about to be opposed to a tiger which he volunteered to encounter almost naked, and armed only with the weapon I have just described. He was rather tall, with a slight figure, but his chest was deep, his arms long and muscular. His legs were thin, yet the action of the muscles was perceptible with every movement; contorrians freedom of his gait and the few whilst the he performed preparatory to the Hazardous enterprise in which he was aboql to cngairet showed that he possessed uncommon activity, combined with no ordinary degree of strength. The expression of his countenance was absolutely sublime when he gave the signal for the tiger to be let loose ; it was the very of concen- tration of moral þÿenergy the index a high

and settled resolution. His body glistened with the oil which had been rubbed over it in order to promote the elasticity of his limbs He raised his arm for several moments above his head when he made the motion to admit his enemy into the area. The bars of a large cage were instantly lilted from above ; a huge r0yal tiger sprang forward and stood before the Coorg, waving his tail slowly backward and forward erecting th® liair upon it, and

Its adversary, fully prepared for this, leaped actively on one side, and as the tiger reached the ground, swung round his heavy knife and brought it w:,n irresistible force upon the animal's hind leg, just above the joint. The bone was instantly severed, and the tiger effectually prevented from making a second spring. The wounded beast roared ; but turning suddenly on the Coorg, who had by this time retired several yards, advanced fiercely upon him, his wounded leg hanging loose in the skin, showing that it was broken. The tiger, now excited to a pitch of reckless rage, rushed forward upon its three legs towards its adversary, w ho stood with his heavy knife upraised, calmly awaiting the encounter. As soon as the savage creature was within his reach, be brought down the ponderous weapon upon its I end with a force which open the skull from ear to ear, and th® vanquished foe fell dead at his feet. EDUCATION IN THE UNITED STATES. The Rev. Andrew Reed, of London, in his 'ate work on America, closes his remarks on the subject of education as follows : I think you cannot fail, my dear friend, to survey this brief report on the subject of education, whether collegiate or common, with wonder and admiration. And yet we have been told, in the face of all this evidence, with petulance and pride, that the Americans have no literature, and are not a literary people þÿ "Not literary ! and yet they have done more for letters than any people ever did in similar circumstances. Not literary ! and yet they have made more extensive grants in favour ot universal education than any other country. Not literary 1 and yet not only the common school, but the academy and the college, are travelling over the breadth of the land; and are sometimes found located in the desert, in anticipation of a race that shall be born. Not literary 1 and yet, in the more settled States, a fourth part of the people are at school ; and in the State of New York alone, apart from all private seminal ies, there are 9,600 schools sustained at a yearly expense of 1,126,488 dollars I Not literary 1 and yet there are, in this new country fifteen universiti- s ; forty-six colleges; twenty-one medical schools ; and twenty-one theological ! Not literary ! and yet they circulate seven hundred and FIFTY MILLIONS of NEWS PAPERS A year, this is twenty-five to our one ; and all our best books commonly run through more and larger editions there than they do

at home. They have no literature, indeed ! The fact is, they have all the literature that is possible to their age and circumstances ; and as these advance, they will assuredly advance in the more abtruce and abstract sciences, till it shall be a bold thing for any to call themselves their peers. Their fidelity for the past is their security for the future .Meantime, arc not Newton and Locke, Bacon anti Shakespear, as much theirs as they are ours? Would it be wisdom, on their part, to repudiate them, even if they had not an equal claim to them ? Would it be wisdom in us to reproach them with tastes which do them honour, and to endeavour to separate them from community in our common republic of letters, which more than any thing may make two great nations, that are one in affinity, one in fact? For my own part, I know of nothing more truly sublime than to see this people in the very infancy ot their national existence, put forth such Herculean energy for the diffusion of universal knowledge and universal virtue 1 But prejudice has neither eyes nor ears !

Emperor of Russia at Vienna. þÿ The Autocrat, about a week ago, dropped one day, as if from the clouds, upon the good people of the Austrian capital, throwing, by his unexpected apparition, the Russian legation into the greatest fright, and the Austrian Court into no inconsiderable embarassment. His smoking horse brought the carriage up to the door of the Hotel of the Embassy, but no bustle met his arrival, & for a considerable time even the bells, which were set a-ringing with fury by the postboys, remained unanswered. The fact was, that no notice bad been given of the þÿEmperor s Other intentions of visiting Vienna, and it was even inown that his post-horses at Prague had been ordered for quite a different direction

ZDJUTSX TSSSTOSTTOSS: maiHHRTOSmS AT23 (such is the custom), no preparations had been made for his reception. þÿ The unfortunate Attack's were mostly in the country amusing themselves, and even the Cliancellerie of Russia was for the nonce all but a desert It happened, however, by some lucky accident, that two remained behind, the Prince Gortschahoff, Councillor, and M. Kondriaffsky, Secretary of Legation, who did their best to give the Emperor a reception Nicholas, however, is good liumeredþÿ he appeared to enjoy the surprise, overlooked all want of form, and made the best of his way to the first dressing-room which he found open There he ordered his baggage to be unpacked, and, after despatching a messenger to Sehcebran to announce his arrival to the Empress Dowager, began to dress for his visit to the Palace. But the people at the latter place were as much taken by surprise as the more humble hangers on of the embassy. The Emperor Ferdinand had not yet arrived from Prague, though he left it before the Autocrat, for his journey was rather retarded by the indisposition of the Empress ; and as Austrian etiquette has no resource in such un-looked-for cases, the marshallers of the courtly ceremonies knew not which way to turn. Expresses were despatched to the Emperor Ferdinand to hasten his return to the capital ; but it was hopeless to expect it, as the Autocrat had declared that he could not wait beyond the same night, or the next morning. A reception was however, got up, the Arch-dukcs Louis and Ferdinand, and such others as were in the

way, were marshalled ; the manner of the Dowager Empress was impressive, and the ceremony passed off well. Whether this visit was a freak of the Czar, a ruse to take the Austrians by surprise, or an affectation of extraordinary vigour and despatch, it seems to have added to the prestige of his being þÿ a great man." þÿ English Paper.

Remar liable Case of Somnambulism. þÿ The good people of Uxbridge have for some time past been kept in a state of no little excitement by a case of somnambulism, which, if we are to credit the accounts that arc given of it þÿ and they are supported by the testimony of witnesses of the most respectable characterþÿ leaves that of Jane Ryder fur in the rear. The subject is a maiden, named þÿ Jillson, of her wonderful powers of þÿvision if indeed no deception is practised þÿ it is said, that she has been able to read with facility any passages, promiscuously selected, from books she had never seen before, when her eyes were first covered with concave leaden caps, made to fit close around the edges, over which were placed thick bats of cotton, and the whole confined in their places, by a bandage of several folds. equally striking instances of the exercise of her powers arc related. The paroxysms have been of frequent occurrence, and have generally happened in the evening.--

Much diversity of opinion exists in the vicinity in relation to this singular case, and o much feeling and interest have been excited by it, that parties have arisen, in which a good portion of the people have ranged themselves, on one side or the other. itcbs®asn&am RELIEF OF ST. SEBASTIAN BY THE BRITISH LEGION. The following important letter was received on Thursday in London, from Major the lion. Fulke Greville, who is next in command to Colonel Arbuthnot, now engaged in the defence of St. Sebastian. The letter is dated St. Sebastian, the 15th December: þÿ I dare say that you will have heard that we are here, and I must put you au. fait as to our position. We landed here on Thursday night from Santander a number of artillerymen, and sent in a chassemaree with two 32-pounders, &,c., and the next morning the remainder of the detachment were landed. Lieutenant Colonel de Lancey, Deputy Adjutant General, Majors Greville, Reyna Isabel Lancers, and þÿM Duff, with the infantry ; Captains Humphrys and Thoreau: Lieuteuants Ridge, Backhouse, Collins; 110 rank and file, with artillery ; Lieutenant Stetterheim ; Cadet Swift; 49 rank and file Reyna Isabel Lancers ; Lieutenant Alvarez, Ensign Muston, 150 rank and file infantry, from the depot ; two 32 pounders, two 24 pounder howitzers, rockets, and a large quantity of ammunition. On Sunday last the truce terminated at twelve þÿo clock, for I must tell you that we learned there was an armistice on the return of the boats of the Isabella on Thursday night. At the last stroke of the bell our artillery opened upon them, well seconded by the Spaniards from the heights ; this continued for about an hour, but there was no reply. There were a few rockets thrown, and almost every shot told. About sunset the Carli.ns fired two guns, which were promptly replied to. þÿ

There was occasional firing during the night, but they threw no shells. The following letter is important, inasmuch as it shows the urgency of relief, and the sense of the inhabitants that it was so promptly thrown in, and i send it translated, to save time : þÿ þÿ Ayuntamiento f o St. Sebastian to the Colonel Commanding the Liritish Auxiliary Forces. fu St. Sebastian, Dec. 13, 1835. þÿ Your happy and prompt arrival with the forces under your command is of the greatest use to this citadel, in the state it was. '1 he protection afforded by these forces is esteemed so much by me and the inhabitants, that I, with the greatest pleasure, do my duty of rendering you homage of the purest thanks ; hut if it was in your power, the Ayuutamiento think it would be most serviceable to have at least 300 more men, till they could be relieved by Spanish troops, and beg of you most strongly to have the goodness to give us this new help, hoping that you will give us all your protection in the present circumstances, because your presence gives confidence, dispels the fears of the inhabitants, and is most useful to the service of Isabel II, and the good j cause. Receive, Sir, the high consideration of my gratitude, « Ai.M. »e Burgue, President, " Lorenzo de Alzate, þÿSecretary. þÿ To Colonel Arbuthnot, þÿ&c.

The Tower of Human Heads in the Island of Jerbi on the Coast of Tunis þÿ In shape (says the writer, Mr. Thomas Kerrich, who visited Jerbi in 1832), the aforesaid monument may be most aptly compared to one of the great þÿants nests ; conical, but not coming to an abrupt point ; from 30 to 35 feet high, and 25 in diameter at its base. The whole consists, or is formed, of human heads, in layers, supported on thigh bones. It appears, that in the first instance, these were simply filled up without any other material, but afterwards emplastered with cement, to preserve the whole from the sea-spray. This is obvious; as, on the side facing the sea, tho cement has, in part, given way, and the skeleton heads are, for a considerable space, exposed to view. I have now in my possession some teeth, extracted in my presence by one of our sailors, who climbed to the top of the tower, using irreverently many an empty mouth with his foot as the steps of a ladder. 1 learned, from ouv Arab pilot, that the tower was called Burj er lloos, and 'hat it is formed of Christian heads ; but as to any thing more, he seemed to think it of no earthly consequence.

A THRILLING DEVELOPEMENT. Our readers may have observed that the lamented death of Mrs. Alston, over which a horrid mystery has hung for many years, has lately again been the subject of newspaper discussion, in consequence of a reported confession of one who had been a pirate. These publications have drawn forth the following apparently authentic statement, which we copy from our latest Mobile paper : From the Mobile Commercial Register. The fate of Mrs, Alston. þÿ I have for some time observed an article going the rounds of the newspapers, in relation to the mysterious death of Mrs. Alston, the daughter of Col. Aaron Burr, taken from the Alabama Journal. This article, although true in many particulars, nevertheless contains several errors, I suppose it grew out of a casual conversation I held in Mr. Smith's Book-store, in Mobile, some six months since, þÿ and as Mr. Smith was very busy at the moment, several gentlemen being in the store, he probably misunderstood me in my statement, þÿ 1st as to the time, and 2ndly as to the receiving the confessions of the pirate, either personally or as a physician. The article was also wrong in many points, as the statement itself will show. I do not charge any one with wilful exaggeration or mis-statement, for nothing is more liable to occur, than for a story to undergo trivial modifications, by frequent repetitions from one individual to another. It is well known under what circumstances Mrs. Alston left South Carolina. Whether she was the only daughter of Col. Burr, I

know not ; but one thing was evident, never did a father love a daughter, or a daughter a parent, with more fervor and devotion than they did. She quit Carolina and embarked at Charleston, with all her effects, consistin' principally of plate, to join him in New York. She sailed, and was heard of no more for years. It is said, her loss afflicted her father more severely than all his political troubles and adversities ; for as before remarked, he loved his daughter. In his last letter to General Wilkinson, written at the most important

The first indication of the nature of Mrs. þÿAlston s death, which had for a long time excited the painful and anxious feelings of her friends and the community, it was said, was communicated in the confessions of a pirate in the neighbourhood of Norfolk, Va. many years since, who stated that the vessel in which she was embarked was seized off the coast of North Carolina, and that Mrs. þÿAlston s That after the crew and passengers of the plate, being considered valuable, caused the murder of all on board, and the robbery of the vessel. I do not know what degree of credit the report obtained. Some years alter this, another man died in South Alabama ; I think it was said to be in Marengo county, who also alluded to the death of Mrs Alston, in the same manner and under the same circumstances, stating that he had been a pirate, and concerned in the transaction ; and that after the vessel was robbed she was scuttled. More recently another had died not very far from Mobile, bearing still stronger testimony in favor of the same horrible transaction. What do all these statements lead to, if they do not all point to the same tragical event ? It is possible that these men wereeach attached to the same piratical crew, and were concerned in the same deed þÿ having subsequently separated and died at different places þÿ suf-

fering torments under the lashings of guilty consciences and fears, pains incident to natural deaths, more awful than deaths infficteu by the halier 1 Col. Burr may doubt, and treat with ridicule these statements, with regard to the lamented fate of his amiable and highly accomplished daughter : and his friends and the commuhity no doubt would cheerfully join him in wishing the death of one so much admired and distinguishes could have been prevented, þÿ or, if death < as inevitable, that it could have happened \ milder means. But, presume, 1 win, the evidence before the community, as to the nature of her late ; however defective it may be, vet in the absence of all other information on that point, must strongly favor the opinion, that she came to her death by the hand ot pirates. Be that as it may, the painful event has passed, and no notice ol it now can do any good. And I, therefore, consider any newspaper notoriety about it, at the present day, unnecessary. It was for this reason, when requested by a friend, to give him the facts in my possession for publication. I declined doing so, alleging that their appearance could answer no useful purpose. But the subject has lately been presented in such a form in the Alabama Journal as to cause me to feel myself called upon to publish this communication, which is done with much reluctance, as mv professional engagements allbrd me little time to devote to such matters. It is not my wish or aim however, to impugn the motives of the Editor of that Journal,

who no doubt acted from correct feelings, concluding every circumstance tending to cast light on that strange atliiir would be interesting to his readers and the public. The pirate who died, and the facts of whr,sc case came into my possession, was b«y the name of Foster. He was without family and kept a grog shop. lie was taci'urn and silent in his disposition. He for sometime before his death grew gradually ty.ore intem-

perate. He often spoke of being a sailor, of having been much at sea, or as the phrase goes, of having seen much þÿservice. He þÿ fell sick, and was confined for some time þÿ His brain appeared disordered, and his mind at times haunted by strange impressions. þÿ v He, on his death bed, confessed to a very worthy and respectable gentleman who stood by him, that he had been a pirate, and belonged to a piratical crew, who took the vessel in which Mrs. Alston had embarked. þÿ

captured vessel were all dispatched, she alone remained to be disposed of. Each man expressed an unwillingness to become her executioner. They finally drew lots, to see whose duty it should be to destroy her ; that it unfortunately fell upon him. Upon learning her fate, she begged strongly and pathetically for her life ; she entreated them to spare her. She told them she was Mrs. Alston, the daughter Aaron Burr, whoJiad been Vice of President ol the United States, and that he was awaiting her in New York, where she was going on to join him, and to console him in his adversity, þÿ that he made her walk the plank, which, finding she could not avert, she finally did, with great firmness and composure !!! He was an illiterate man, and had probably never read any thing on the subject. For some days previous to his death, he imagined he saw her in his room, and would convulsively point to different parts of the chamber, exclaiming with much earnestness þÿ þÿ There, there she is þÿ/ and would ask the bystanders if they did not sec her. This delusion tormented him as long as he could make himself understood, when lie died a most miserable death 1 In corroboration of this statement, the testimony of several gentlemen could be mentioned, whose standing and character arc of the first order in the community, and whose veracity, where known, never will be questioned, and who know the above statement to ' be substantially true ; but I have no authority for calling them by name. If Col. Burr should

yet doubt on the subject, evidence could be adduced, to establish it in any court of justice, which, being a lawyer, lie would be obliged to admit. I do not consider it necessary to be more minute on the subject, unless 1 should be formally called on by some one, who has authority, or claims for more particular information. Because, as before observed, nothing of the kind can do any good-further dcvelopement and discussion can only tend to revive melancholy feelings and unpleasant regrets, which time had measurably buried in oblivion. ALEXANDER JONES, M. D. Mobile, Alabama, July lit, 1833.

LONDON. ( From the Morning Herald , Dec. 19) It is with some degree of satisfaction we find there is now a certainty of an Hospital being established for aged, disabled, and decayed Masters, mates and Seamen employed in the merchant navy of the United Kingdom, and we trust that it will be supported in a manner becoming the service. A seaman is the most thoughtless of beings when on shore, with his pockets filled with his hard-earned wages, and His sole endeavour appears to be how to get rid of his cash in the most unsatisfactory manner to himself. There are few instances of sailors putting by any thing against a stormy day, and it therefore behoves shipowners to exert themselves to provide for those who expend strength in bringing wealth to their stores. Within the last few weeks a plan for a þÿSavings Bank for sailors has been proposed, and if it prove successful, it will assist to raise the character of the British seaman, by inducing them to look to the future. The hospital and the þÿSavings Bank will have a beneficial effect, and we strongly recommend shipowners to suggest to sailors, when they pay them offi to subscribe to the Hospital, and place as much of their pay in the Bank, as their immediate wants do not require him to expend. Let sailors once witness the establishment of such an institution as the Hospital, and let them sec the worn-out mariner elothed and maintained in comfort, and it will be strange if the sympathies of our tars be not excited.

Our observations upon the Message of the American President to Congress having been written on Wednesday night, before the arrial of the Speech of the Iv;ng of the French to the Chamber of Deputies, we were not aware of the official announcement of the fact that the British Government has offered its mediation between the Governments of France and America. We therefore put the subject hypothetically. THE WAR IN FLORIDA, The letter we subjoin from Lieut. VV. H. Bulloch, editor of the Savannah Georgian, and at present serving in Florida, throws a clear light cn the critical affairs of that territory. Camp Charles Omatiila, ) Picolata, Florida, E. Jan. 6. 1836. $ Dear Sir þÿ Since my last, nothing of very great importance has occurred. Our men have begn busily engaged the whole of the past week in cutting poles for pickets, ditching, &c. &.c. To-day, at noon, the pickets were completed þÿ and wo are now enclosed in a fortification of pine logs, which will resist the incursions of the Indians and all their efforts, long enough, at any rate, to aliord us time to awake from our slumbers and arm for defence. As a body, the Volunteers from Savannah, who, with two or three more individuals, compose the defence of this place, are entitled to great credit, for they have labored cheerfully every day, felling pine trees, ditching, &c &c. until the buildings were enclosed by bastions, pickets, <kc. We have two brass six-pounders mounted, and well charged witli cannister and grape, and upwards of forty men determined to protect the place, or perish in the attempt. Wc so far, I am satisfied, owe our safety to our vigilance, having a strong guard set every night, every man performing alternately every third day and night sentinel duty. We have, doubt, less, for some days, had Indians prowling

The driver of the Stage between this place and St. Augustine, who was expected here yesterday at 2 þÿo clock, did not arrive until just one þÿo clock to day and then on horseback ; the persons, six in numbei, who had engaged to come as passengers to this place, being detericd by the reported presence ol Indians in the vicinity of the road. It seems that a party of about eighteen, fired upon a white man namej , on Monday evening last, at a place about seven miles from this, and killed liim. A small negro hoy, who was with him, fled, and though closely pursued by the Indians, succeeded in etfecting his escape by entering a swamp, and favored bv the approach of night, reached St. Augustine in their ty. The driver, yesterday, observed safemoccasin tracks across the road from St Augustine to Picolata. On the arrival of the steamboat this evening from Savannah, we advised the Captain to anchor in the stream opposite our pickets, which he did. We expect momently to sec their tires blaze from þÿ the store house at the steamboat landing, which is about a quarter of mile above us, or gleam from other buildings in the vicinity. The man mentioned above as killed hv them, was one of a small force ot five or six whom we found stationed her- on our arrival. They were on Friday last ordered off to Mosquito and St. Augustine. The inhabitants of St. Augustine are, we learn, very much alarmed. Several strangers there areanxi

ous to leave it. A party of four trom the volunteers sent to Alusquito, arrived yesterday morning at St. Augustine, hut state that the volunteers winch left St Augustine under Gen. Hernandez, had not yet met with the Indians. The inhabitants at St Augustine, 1 here, have commenced to picket the town. January, 7. Although it poured a deluge most of last night, we heard or saw nothing oi the Indians. We emphatically slept on our arms, some of the men not even taking off' their caps. The more 1 see oi our men, the more pleased am I with their soldierly conduct. Llrenched as the sentinels last night were to the skin, i have heard trom them no murmurs, bui they, one and all, though lew of them have e'er before shouldered a musket, evince all the esprit of the soldier. 1 hey have the proud consciousness of believing that but for their presence. Picolata would on Monday night last, if not sooner, have been laid in ashes As an individual, this belief compensates me tor the sacrifices I have made, m common with others. If the opportunity for action is allowed us we hope to give a good account el these sav- ages. WE FREDERIK THE SIXTH, by the Grace of God, King of Denmark, the V, nds and Goths, Duke of'Slesvig, Holstein, Stormarn, Ditrnarsk, Luuenborg and Oldenborg, MAKE KNOWN: That notwithstanding it had already been prescribed by an Ordinance respecting the hlave trade, given by our late father of blessed memory, and dated on the 16th of March 1702, that all such trade was to cease from the year 1803 for our royal subjects, as well on the coast of Africa, as in other places where it might exist, besides in Our Royal Colonics in the Westindies, and that after the expiration of the said term, no male nor female Negro should be allowed to be purchased by or for the Royal subjects, nor to be shipped on board of vessels belonging to our Royal subjects, nor to be carried to the Royal Westindia Islands to be sold there, and that all trade contrary to this Law should from that tiinc be considered as illegal, VVe have still, after having been invited by His Majesty the King of the French and His Majesty the King of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, to join the conventions, which have been concluded by the said Powers under dates ot the 30th of November 1831, and the 22nd of March 1833, for the suppression of the traffic in slaves, been willing to unite Our exertions with theirs, in order to take the most effectual means to suppress the said trade. In giving further publicity through this Our Ordinance to the said Conventions, to which we have

LAST HOURS OF JOHN RANDOLPH. The Richmond Courier contains the following copy of the deposition of Dr. Parrish, the physician who attended the late John Randolph in his last moments. It was read before the General Court at Richmond, during the trial of the Will of the deceased: þÿ Joseph Parrish, of the City of Philadelphia Doctor of Medicine, aged fifty-five years or thereabouts, being produced, affirmed and examined on behalf of William Meade, named to the annexed commission, deposeth as follows : That being legally required to make a deposition relative to John Randolph of Roanoke, I hereby state my recollection of such incidents as I consider calculated to show the state of his mind during the period of my medical attendance. þÿ John Randolph died under my medical care on the morning of the fifth month, (May) twenty fourth, eight hundred and thirty-three, at one quarter before twelve o'clock. He breathed his last in a chamber of the City Hotel, No. 41 North Third street. I was present at his departure, closed his eyes and placed his limbs in a decent position. I was called to visit him on the twentieth of said month by Edmund Badger, one of the proprietors of the City Hotel. It was a stormy night þÿ the patient had arrived that afternoon in the steamboat from Baltimore. He was bound for Europe, and had been disappointed in getting on board the packet. He soon informed me that he was acquainted with me by character, I know you through þÿGiles þÿ alluding, I presume, to William B. Giles, late Governor of Virginia, respecting whose case

I was repeatedly consulted. The patient appeared much disturbed, on account of some dilliculties he had encountered after leaving the steamboat. It was evident .» v woe C A -tremeiv ill : his debiffi- þÿ , . . .j was such, that it was with great difficulty he could expectorate, which caused much distress in respiration. þÿ He appeared fully aware of his danger, þÿ told me he had attended several courses of lectures on Anatomy, þÿ described his symptoms with medical accuracy, declaring he must die if he could not discharge the puriform matter. On enquiring how long he had been sick, he replied, þÿDon t þÿ ask me that question ; I have been sick all my life." He soon told, however, that he had been affected for three years with his present disease, which had been greatly aggravated by his voyage to Russia þÿ this had killed him On feeling his pulse, he said, You can form no þÿ judgment of my pulse it is so þÿpeculiar. I soon perceived, that to manage the case before me would be like steering between Scylla and Gharybuis, and concluded to proceed by cautious soundings, rather than advance under full sail. « I told him he had been so long an invalid he must have acquired an accurate knowledge c the general course of practice adapted to his case. He replied, þÿ certainly, at forty a fool or a physician, you þÿknow. I remarked there were idiosyncrasies in many constitutions, and wished to ascertain what was peculiar about him. Dog and Horse. þÿ The following is an instance of the sensibility, if l may call it so, of a horse, and proves, how alive he is to danger. A friend of mine was riding a horse one day in India, attended by a spaniel dog, who had long been its companion. The dog ran into some long grass, and came out crying and shaking its head; the horse, contrary to his usual custom, not only avoided the dog, but showed the utmost dread of its coming near him ; the dog soon died, and, upon examining him, it was found that he heal been bitten in the tongue by a venomous snake.

Her tongue still chats of this and that, Than aspine leaf it wags more fast ; And as she talks she knows not what, There issues many a ruthless blast.
Thou far dost take thy mark amiss, If thou think faith in them to find: The weather-cock more constant is, Which turns about with every wind.
I know some pepper-nosed dame Will term me fool and saucy jack, That dare their credit so defame, And lay such slanders on their back.
What though on me they pour their spite : I may not use the gloser's trade, I cannot say the crow is white, But need must call a spade a spade. 0 0 To the Virgins, to make much
of time. robert merrick þÿ (Bom 1591.) Gether ye rosebuds while ye may, Old Time is still a flying ; And this same flower that smiles to-day. To-morrow will be dying.
The glorious lamp of Heaven, the Sun, The higher he's a getting, The sooner will his race be run, And nearer he's to setting.
That age is best which is the first, When youth and blood are warmer. But, being spent, the worse, and worst Times, still succeed the former.
Then be not coy, but use your time, And, while ye. may, go marry ; For, having lost but once your prime, You may for ever tarry.

ON WHAT DOES HAPPINESS DEPEND? a quoi tiknt bomleull , " Le bonheur ne tient souvent qu'a n cheveu.' We are indebted to the columns of Lin dependent, published in New-Orleans, for the happiness is held by us as human bipeds, " by is termed liberal translation is designedly of that order which following. We must state, for the satisfaction of those who peruse the original, that the I have heard it said by some persons, that . a thread." The Engiish author Dr. Young, says of human existence þÿ " Tlie spider's most attenuated thread Is cord, is cable, to the slender tie We bold on human life " How much more true of happiness whilst we live ? Others say, that instead of a thread, it is held by nothing. Other®, again, that it may be found and held, in every thing, and by every thing. I believe, that the great matter is to hold it properly. Happiness itself, in the abstract, 1 believe to be a mere chimera. I have sought it þÿ shall I tell you where? every where. And, as the best, though forlorn, hope, I sought it in the heart of women. Pardon me, ladies ! It may be owing to the dale at which 1 was born, that I believe your sex will forgive neither the errors of age, nor those ol youth. I believe that it is seldom you love at ail. Nay more, so strongly convinced am I of your inconstancy, even if you could love, and so well do I remember the consequences which resulted from the fault of my father, in having me born at the close of the eighteenth century, that, unless you beg me not, I am almost induced to say »»

I was born in a romantic country village, but, not caring to make myself very interesting to you, I shall speak neither of murmuring brooks, nor of birds " chanting the green leaves beneath." The brooks no longer murmur for me ; the birds no longer sing ; my green leaves of Spring are turning yellow. 1 am thirty- four years old. And when a man is thirty-four years old þÿ for him, believe me, ladies, if he be not of a peculiar tenperament, but has travelled and filled public stations þÿ he cares little about singing, or being sung to ; still less about murmuring brooks." I, for my own part, would not give a cent for the murmurs of all the brooks in the world. I have enough to do to murmur myself. Happiness is a "Racine and every one knows the epithet bestowed by the " romantiques," on this prince of elegiac poets. þÿ Happiness, is, in fact, like a jester. I misunderstand him, and then I am vexed with him: sick of him. He gives me nausea. þÿ 1 wish to have no more of happiness. I believe no longer in its existence. 1 never have believed. It is an imposture ! Do you doubt this ? Then hear my þÿstory s a tory sufficient to make savages, aye, brutes, the most ferocious brutes shed tears. During fifteen long years 1 lived in a pool of water, as it were supplied by my own eyes. So abundant, indeed were my tears, that my philanthrophy made me uneasy. 1 feared the world would be visited with another deluge. Whatever it was that put it into my head to fall in love I cannot tell Believe me, gen-

tle reader, on my soul, my falling in love was no act of mine. But I loved. Am I asked how I knew that 1 loved ? I will tell y. ,u. When I was near the adored one I w M un. happy, for 1 feared she loved mc not. When

distant I was more unhappy still. The sight of her set my blood in a boiling state and not to see her distracted my bosom Many was the sad day I passed þÿ many the long, the sleepless night. My hair was turning grey. This, by the by was the only traitor to the secret ; for, should I have told you, I loved in silence. In silence! Yes, in silence to her I loved, whilst in the depth of my own heart I heard the roar of a very tempest of love. It was one evening, at that hour when the features of a lady may with impunity " give the lie" (excuse me my fair readers) to her voice before the candles were lighted, one evening was it, that the tones of my Dulcinea appeared to respond in those of " love for love." I saw (of course) no smile, mocking the accents of her lips, no glance of her eye in the shade of that apartment, showing how little she thought of my plaints 1 saw nothing, I heard nothing, but that voice, which seemed to assure me I was beloved as I loved. As if by accident, she asked my age. " I am twenty-eight," I replied, and I said so in such a state of unconsciousness, that I might as probably have said fifty But " " the thought of that scene is too much for me ! It was at the moment 1 tmade this answer, lost to every thing. I had but one thought. It was of her, who veiled in the darkness of the apartment sat beside me. It was settled that we were to be married on the morrow. I will not recount all the rollies which in the overflow of joy, contemplating the proximity and certainty of so much

happiness, I committed. They are easily imagined. Every thing was ready, the requisite purchases made ; the " wedding garb" put in order ; the rooms were garlanded ; the ball room figured ; no expense were spared ; in short, I was about to be perfectly happy. þÿ Certain am that the I, magistrate who was to perfect my felicity (it was the worthy major of the fifth arrondissement) will never forget the scene for the remainder of his life. He missed it by the finest attack of dyspepsia, (from overfeasting) which has been known in Paris for half a century. We had proceeded as far in the ceremony as that part in which I had to declare my age : þÿ Thirty four years 1" " Thirty-four 1" exclaimed my wife-that was-about-to-be, " why you told me twentyeight 1" "It may be so, Miss; but yon know we know not what we say, when in love." My future better half affectionately answered thus: "Well, sir, when men know not what they say, it is time for women to know what they do! Your servant, sir, 1 shall riot marry to a man of thirty-four, for'example." I thought this was too much, particularly the latter words, " for example." I told her so. She was about to quit the place. Her father remonstrated with her, on the impropriety of her conduct. All in vain 1 She grew still more angry, and remonstrated with her father. In the midst of her anger she gave an inconsiderate jerk to one of her ringlets. þÿ That head of hair which had entangled my heart ! It all came ofl'; (It was a wig) and a

bald young lady stood before me ! The scene was so droll that I could not repress my laughter. 1 was cured ol my passion ; and shall now die contented a bachelor. On what depends then, human happiness. Often it hangs by a hair !

THE SLOUCHED þÿHAT a true story. In the year 10 þÿ , there appeared in the goodly town of Boston, one Monsieur le Cain, who, from the account he gave of himself, came to sojourn among them for the purpose of instructing the sober and steady citizens in the " noble science of defence." He took lodgings in King street, at the sign of the Cat and Parrot, from whence he issued his cards ; giving notice that at all hours of tlie day, he held himself in readiness at his room to give lessons in the noble exercise of the broad sword. This boast at once drew forth the pride and feeling of all the young blades in town who had ever " don'd glove" or handled foil ; and many in consequence were the encounters with the dapper Frenchman. It was all in vain, the skill and activity of Mon-ieur carried him through all triumphant : This success tickled his pride, and to gratify his vanity, or more perhaps to extend his celebrity, and to increase the number of his pupils, he caused a stage to be erected on the common, upon which he daily appeared, armed " cap a pie," giving challenge that he was ready then and there to contend with naked blades against all new comers. the town but to face this gunpowder Captain of the Louises in mortal combat, was not for a moment to be thought of. No one ever dreamt of attempting it. Thus Monsieur Le Cain had his stage entirely to himself, upon which fie continued daily to renew his challenge, give point and cut direct upon the empty air. It was at one of those daily exhibitions, when an unusually large number were looking on to witness his dexterity in cutting and flourishing, and listening to the often repeated challenge, that a man stept out from the crowd, and very coolly walking forward, drew I lis glove from his hand and cast it upon the platform, in token of his acceptance of the cnaileiige. This self possession was noticed by Le Cain, and tended to increase his rage : he shifted his ground, and attempted to bring the face of his antagonist to the sun, his opponent turned to receive him as steadily as if he moved upon a pivot, continuing to act only on the defensive. the blessinos of a " liberal" government. On the 1 9th of October four ruffians belonging to a gang of assassins in Lisbon, and headed by a sergeant of the 5th Cavalry, broke into the house of the Mareschal de Campo Antonio JoaquimBandeira atGullegao, and murdered him in the most savage manner, in the presence of his wife and eight children ! This is the fourth General Officer who has fallen under the poinards of the assassins since the restoration. The others were Thiago Pedro Martins and Ricardo Paulo Soares, both Major Generals and both murdered at Serpa, in the Alemtejo; and Major-General Thomas Antonia Cabreira, murdered at Tavira, in the Algarves. Lieut.- General the Visconde, de St. Joao da Pesqueira, on his way to the common gaol, had a narrow escape from the daggers of the same gang. The Visconde, who is universally beloved by the inhabitants of Pesqueira, is actually confined in the Euxovia, a sort of black hole, a gaol of the lowest and most filthy description, where the worst of criminals only are immured. The actors in these dismal tragedies are the emissaries of certain Liberal Clubs in Lisbon, who devote to destruction every one who served in the army of Hon Miguel. They are perfectly well known, yet no steps arc taken to punish their crimes ; and under these circumstances it is not wonderful that it should be currently reported and believed that they are now in the pay of the Government itself. Their victims are among the most popular men in the country ; men

whose only crime was that of loyalty to their sovereign, and whose only folly was that of putting some faith in the promises and professions of " Liberals." The same perfidy and the same savage cruelty characterise the revolutionist everywhere. May we never have to rue his ascendency in England. þÿ United Service Gazette.
