Groq versus Water. þÿ It is rather a singular coincident, and one which probably might not again occur for the next fifty years, that the day (yesterday) on which the Act for retailing Rum and other Spirituous Liquors came into full operation, there was a meeting of the Temperance Society held. Whether it was as numerously attended as ori former similar occasions, we know not ; but this we are certain of, that those persons who deal in the sale of intoxicating liquors, such as before mentioned, seemed more busied in preparing to vend them, by complying with what the law requires than in trying to persuade people against drinking grog. Temperance is certainly a great virtue, and should be cherished in every society, but we think the age of sensuality has almost passed by, and even the most ignorant begin to feel that they are under a moral obligation not to destroy their health by the intemperate use of strong liquor. Besides, we would ask in a moral point of view, where the difference is between the man who drinks but is never drunk, and he who does not drink? which of the two is the most dangerous enemy to society ? There is no difference, and if so, it is sufficiently plain, without further argument, that temperance, in the moral sense of the word, does not imply a total abstinence from strong liquor. Much praise is due to all who endeavour to turn those who are going wrong from the error of their ways, but sometimes the best and wisest prompters of a good thing mistake both the time and object. It is a

question whether morality would suffer more from a philosopher w ho, like Arcesilaus, decried it by his words, but supported it by his deeds, or from him who, like Aristippus, gave sobriety his praise, but sensuality his practice. Without meaning any improper comparison, we may add, that some preceptors, perceiving this dilemma, have run upon both the horns of it in endeavouring to escape them, and have taught us what we ought to do by their precept, and what we ought not to do by their example.

Anecdotes of þÿWashington. On one occasion, General Stone, while travelling across the country with his family, found it necessary to cross a ferry belonging to Washington, and offered the ferryman a moidore in payment. The man refused it, saying that he had no means of weighing it, which his master would most assuredly do ; and in case it should fall below the standard weight, the loss, as well as the displeasure of Washington, would be visited upon him. Gen Stone upon this offered the man threepence more to compensate for every possible deficiency of weight. þÿ The ferryman received and duly paid it to his employer. On weighing it, it was found to be below weight to the value of three halfpence, upon which Washington wrapped up the remaining 3 half-pencc, and remitted it to General Stone. U pon another occasion, while Washington was from home, a room in his house was plastered by his order. On his return he measured the room, and on inspecting the workman's account, discovered that he had charged fifteen shillings more than was due. Some time after the plasterer died, and his wife married another man, who advertised in the provincial newspapers that he was ready to pay and receive all that was due from or to his wife's former husband. Washington, on seeing the paper, immediately substantiated his claim for the fifteen shillings, and received the amount ! þÿ E dmond't Life and Times, 4c.

FARIETI E S. þÿr þÿ - þÿ þÿ þÿ DE TOCQUEVILLE ON DEMOCRACY IN AMERICA. The crowd of English politicians, whether public men or public writers, who live in a truly insular ignorance of the great movement of European ideas, will be astonished to find, that a conclusion which but few among them, in their most farreaching speculations have yet arrived at, is the point from which the foremost continental thinkers begin theirs ; and that philosopher, whose impartiality as between aristocracy and democracy is unparalleled in our time, considers it an established truth, on the proof of which it is no longer necessary to insist, that the progress of democracy neither can nor ought to he stopped. Not to determine whether democracy shall come, but how to make the best of it when it does come, is the scope of M. de þÿTocqueville s speculations. That comprehensive survey of the series of changes composing the history of our race, which is now familiar to every continental -writer with any pretensions to philosophy, has taught to M. de Tocqueville, that the movement towards democracy dates from the dawn of modern civilization, and has continued steadily advancing from that time. Eight centuries ago, society was divided into barons and serfs ; the barons being every thing, the serfs nothing. At every succeeding epoch this inequality of condition is found to have somewhat abated :þÿ every century has done something considerable towards lowering the powerful and raising the low. Every

step in þÿcivilization every victory of intellect -ever advancement in wealth þÿ has multiplied the resources of the many ; while the same causes, by their indirect agency, have frittred away the strength and relaxed the energies of the few. VVe now find ourselves in a condition of society which, compared with that whence we have emerged, might be termed equality : yet not only are the same levelling influences still at work, but their force is vastly augnfented by new elements which the world never before saw. For the first time, the power and habit of reading begins to permeate the hitherto inert mass. Reading is power ; not only because it is knowledge, hut still more because it is a means of communiþÿcation because, by the aid of it, not only do opinions and feelings spread to the multitude, but every individual who holds them knows that they are held by the multitude ; which of itself suffices, if they continue to be held, to ensure their speedy predominance. The many, for the first time, have now learned the lesson, which, once learned, is never forgotten þÿ that their strength, when they chuse to exert it, is invincible. And, for the first time, they have learned to unite for their own objects, without waiting for any section of the aristocracy to place itself at their heqd The capacity ol co operation for a common purpose, heretofore a monopolized instrument of power in the hands of the higher classes, is now a most formidable one in the hands of the lowest. Under these influences it is not sur-

prising, that society makes greater strides in ten years, towards the levelling of inequalities, than lately in a century, or formerly in three or four. M. de Tocqueville is unable to imagine that a progress, which has continued with uninterrupted steadiness for so many centuries, can be stayed now. He assumes that it will continue, until all artificial inequalities shall have disappeared among mankind ; those inequalities only remaining which arc the natural and inevitable effects of the protection of property þÿ London Review.

'»- litJ 4iu l<>MU4MUMHilai£aM«MM» J« , QUACKERY. About the year 1782 tliere appeared in London a physician, wlio soon made himself extremely remarkable. This man, whose name was Graham., was a graduate of Edinburgh. He wrote in a nervous, though sometimes bombastic style, and was extremely elegant in his address. Dr. Graham opened an establishment in Pallmall, to which he gave the sounding title of þÿ An enormous Sun, brightly gill, a statue of Hygeia (the Goddess of health), and other conspicuous emblems of the þÿDoctor vocation, s adorned the entrance. Within might be seen a suite of rooms magnificently furnished, the walls covered with mirrors, and all objects heaped together profusion in that could lead the visitor to imagine himself in an enchanted palace. Here it was that Dr. Graham delivered his lectures on health ; and particularly on all that relates to the propagation of our species. His terms were two guineas a lecture, and strange as it may appear, numbers flocked to hear him ; some attracted by the novelty of the subject, others expecting something extraordinary from the magnitude of the charge. The doctor did not rely altogether on his own effects to obtain success. With him resided a tall handsome woman, who assumed the title of þÿ Goddess of þÿHealth. Her business was to address the audience at the termination of the lecture. As auxiliary means of attraction, two men of gigantic stature were employed to preambulate the town, and carry about the þÿDoctor c s ards. Their dress contributed to render them conspicuous.

An enormous three cornered hat, and a heavy and peculiar livery, excited general notice. þÿ In the course of time, however, the audience at two guineas became less numerous. The price was lowered to half the sum, and after some time was reduced to half a guinea, and then to five shillings, and half a crown; to allow all, as the Doctor expressed it, to benefit by his wonderful and peculiar views. In his list of curious articles was a certain bed richly covered and ornamented, standing on legs glass, of which the Doctor called þÿ Diþÿvine. He asserted that persons joined together by the marriage bond, but to whom oilsprings was denied, could obtain that blessing by making use of his magic couch. The charge, for a single night for his bed, was 100 guineas ; and though the sum was enormous so great is the folly of fortune, united to prodigality, that many persons of elevated rank were found to have made trial of the talisman. The Doctor professed also to have the secret of the elixir vitae. He asserted, that by his aid life could be prolonged to the utmost limit of the wildest wish, and for this invaluable boon he only demanded 1,000 guineas. It is said that more than one wealthy person paid the sum, but the dose could not have been sufficiently potent, for all who took it in order to live for ever, have long since been numbered with the dead. At last, Dr. Graham began to perceive that public, curiosity was on the wane, the þÿ Temple of þÿHealth was deserted, and the þÿgoddess was no longer worshipped.

Thu Duke op Orleans. þÿ On the Duke of Orleans landing at Algiers, he was addressed by the Mayor, and his answer confirmed hopes that his arrival on this coast, þÿ to remain the for ever hereafter part of þÿFrance (the words of the Mayor), had created. The Mayor, in the name of himself and the other municipal authorities, presented to his Royal Highness a remarkably fine Arabian courser, with a bridle and saddle of the country, and covered with a housing of silk, richly worked with silver and gold, similar to that which usually v'as put on the horse of the Dey. Upon this horse the Prince made his entry into that city. The Moorish inhabitants of Algiers were much flattered by the Duke of Orleans having chosen for his residence the house of a native, Mustapha Pacha, which was prepared for the þÿPrince s reception in a style of splendid hospitality. The whole of the first story appropiated to his Royal Highness, Mustapha reserving to himself and his women only the ground floor. Fountains of water,' fragrant flowers, polished marbles the richest carpets, in short, all the luxury of the East, and ail the indulgences the nature of the climate dictates were combined with prodigality in the mansion of Mustapha. The outside of this building, like all the great houses of the East, is of a gloomy and mean appearance, and thus heightened the effect found in the interior. The þÿPrince s visit to Buffarick was marked by a singular occurrence. A young negro woman, who was unable to bear any longer the ill-

treatment she received from her master, fled, and took refuge in the camp, a few days before the þÿDuke sarrival. The moment he reached the camp the negrees threw herself at his feet, and at the same time the master came forward and claimed her as his property. His Royal Highness could not resist the distress of the poor woman, nor did he wish to violate rights of property established by the custom of the country, and, therefore, he bargained with the rnastei for his slave, and purchased her. Not knowing what to do with his new acquisition, the Duke of Orleans offered to give a dower with her to any free negro who would marry her. A quarter master of the regiment of Spalus came forward and agreed to take her for his wife : the dower was given, and the two blacks went rejoicing together to Algiers, and were married at the grand mosque. This, and other acts, showing the great and discriminating goodness of the heart of his Royal Highness, have rendered him popular with the natives, who at the same time admire his expressive countenance, his martial air, his tall and manly person, the grace with which he displays his horsemanship, and the tone with which he gives the word of þÿcommand. Difficulty of procuring Medical Assistance. þÿ The impossibility of procuring prompt medical aid, in passing through the country between the European stations, forms a cruel aggravation to the distress of the companions of those who may be taken ill upon a journey. A newly married bride embarked with her husband, who belonged to the civil service of the Company, on board a budgerow, with the intent to proceed to Patna, where he had received an appointment. The bridegroom attacked by illness upon the river, while at a considerable distance from any European dwelling, languished for a few hours and then expired. The servants endeavoured to persuade the sorrowing widow to permit them to land the body, and have it interred in the jungle ; but to this she would not consent, and immediately betaking themselves to the baggage-boat, they left her alone with the corpse. Instead of proceeding on a voyage, whose object had been defeated by the death of the principal person of the party, it was deemed advisable to turn the head of the boat round, and go down the river. The wind unfortunately was adverse, and, notwithstanding the strength of the current, the vessel made little progress. Imagination cannot picture anything more horrible than the office which devolved upon one who remained faithful even in death. The following Message was received from the President of the United States. To the Senate and House of Representatives : The Government of Great Britain has offered its mediation for the adjustment of the

Carefully guarding that point in the controversy, which, as it involves our honor and independence, admits of no compromise, I have cheerfully accepted the offer. It will be obviously improper to resort even to the mildest measures of a compulsory character, until it is ascertained whether France has declined or accepted the mediation. 1 therefore recommend a suspension of all proceedings on that part of my Special Message of the 15th of January last, which proposes a partial non-intercourse w ith France. While we can. not too highly appreciate, the elevated and disinterested motives of the oiler of Great Britain, aud have a just reliance upon the great influence of that power to restore the relations of ancient friendship between the U. States and France, and know, too, that our own pacific policy will be strictly adhered to until the national honor compels us to depart Horn it, wc should be insensible to the exposed

condition of our country, and forget the lessons of experience, if we did not efficiently and sedulously prepare for an adverse result. The peace of a nation does not depend exclusively upon its own will, nor upon the beneficent policy of neighboring powers, and that nation which is found totally unprepared for the exigencies and dangers of war, although it come without having given warning of its approach, is criminally negligent of its honor and its duty. I cannot too strongly repeat the recommendation, already made, to place the seabord in a proper state for defence, and promptly to provide the means for amply protecting our commerce. ANDREW JACKSON.

S.) which developed a good many curious family matters, and furnished much amusement to those who have a taste for the uncurtaining of marital mishaps, Mrs. Vance instituted proceedings against her husbagd, Mr. Vance, for the purpose of obtaining, in the first place, a divorce ; and, secondly, a competent alimony from the pocket of her cara spnsa. The " male creature" in the suit was a poor old gentleman of some 70 winters, who had some time before taken into his head to marry a young wife of only 20. The lady's inducement to become a party to this frosty transaction was stated with great delicacy and succinctness by herself þÿ she married Mr. Vance for his money, and upon the principle that " the hide and tallow of an old ox, would buy a young steer any time." Mrs. Vance, however, seemed tired of waiting for the " hide'1 of her husband in the ordinary course of nature, and sought some of the " tallow" through the instrumentality of the law. She brought her suit accordingly. The charges against Vance were extreme cruelty. He had bruised, bitten, kicked, pinched, thumped, and pushed his better half. All this she proved, On the other hand the venerable respondent proved that his wife was in the habit of leaving her bed at night to smoke a cigar ! The lady, however, met this by a replication. She brought testimony to prove that he had a most unhusband-

ly fondness for cats, and was, moreover, addicted to onions. This last enormity, we believe, settled the case. The Court could not stand that, but immediately granted a divorce a mensa et thoro ; ordered the husband to pay 100 dollars by way of costs, and the yearly sum of two hundred dollars during the lady's life for her maintenance, payable quarterly.

A Genuine Giiost Story. þÿ The following is from the ' Journal of the heart," by the late Airs. Darner, edited by Lady Charlotte Bury ; is given as genuine: þÿ A Mr. Cox (commonly called Jumper Cox) being at Lady Bother's, near Oxford, was desired by her to pronounce a few Latin sentences by way of persuading her servants, who suppose the house to be haunted, that he was a conjuror, and had banished the ghost to the Bed Sea " \ ou must excuse me," said he, " for, in truth, 1 am not myself convinced of the absurdity of such persuasions : and my reason is because 1 once fancied that 1 saw my mother in-law come to my bedside and undraw the curtains ; she then told me that my wife would die before the end of the year. « As for myself,' she added, you will never see again, for I was now !' The next morning 1 hastened to Wallingford, where my mother in law resided ; I found that she had been seized with a contagious fever, had died, and had been buried immediately exactly on the night and at the hour which the ghost had mentioned. I wished to have had the coffin opened ; but the clergyman representing that it could be of no service, and might create great discontent among the populace, 1 desisted But what surprised me much was, that, though I mentioned the circumstance to no one but the clergyman, whose interest it was to conceal it, several weeks afterwards a young lady in a distant part of the county said to inc. þÿ ' Bless me, Mr. Cox, 1 had the strangest dream
last night. I thought your mother in-law came to tnv bedside, and told me ll at she had been buried alive at Wallingford.'

A chieftain in India is not esteemed completely conquered, ev< n if he should fall in battle in the vain attem it to resist an invader, until his oppoi nt si. ad have numbered die women ol the ana amongst his willing slaves; triumph a which has seldom been achieved. I hese proofs of conquest have always been deemed worthy ot record, either in the page of history, or a stone monument erected in commemoration ol so proud an event ; but while such chronicles are rare, there is scarcely a family ot note in Indi i which cannot produce some testimonial of the determination ot the women to sustain the honour of their male relatives at the expense of their own lives. Alen about to engage in hopeless sotion, have often commenced by putting all the females ot their zenanas to the sword, the women yielding as a matter of course; and, in other instances, when defeat has unexpectedly ensued, the intelligence of the approach of the conqueror has almost invariably been met by the voluntary sacrifice of the women, rather than submit to pass, like house hold onods. from one master to another. In these licides there never has been known a dissentient voice ; all have cheerfully on# countered death, falling in heaps upon the ground ; the mother, with her daughters, the wives, concubines, and slaves, animated by one impulse, and regarding a premature grave as nothing compared to a life of dishonour. þÿ Instances are well known, in wliieh the women have killed themselves in order to enable

the males of the family to escape from the toils of an enemy. Where a retreat encumbered by females would have been hopeless, they have cleared the way by the only expedient which honour could sanction. Tragedies of this kind have been enacted over and over again: nor are they confined to a bygone age of chivalry. In all the independent states, where despotism still prevails, and British law, precept, and example, have not as yet interposed their salutary influence as a restraint upon the conduct of a people whoso virtues are of a bai baric stamp, lite women are as ready us c\ei to uestroy themselves, when death appears nocessnn fur th<- pieservaiiuu ut family honour. þÿ Atiutic Journal.

LOVE AND DISCRETION. From thirty downwards men calculate in proportion to the force of f heir attachment. þÿ They imagine probabilities of a failure which never rise on a young man's brain. He proceeds as it were by instinct, and every step he takes is rather the effect of accident than design. But they deliberate on each detail. They weigh their words. They watch lor Opportunities. And it is thus that so many young women, especially of my heroine's stamp, are attracted and caught, they know not why or how, and to the great wonderment of shallow observes, by suitors discrepant in various ways besides enters into the daring adventure, with all the odds against him, what are the chances, what the compensation? The impetuous burst of boyish fancy is incomparably less interesting than the delicate, yet manly march of matured passion Whoever has left the first may be allowed to imagine the latter : to picture himself the full grown mind, with reason, taste, and sentiment united, choosing its object, and firmly careering on its way ; each day growing bolder and tenderer, but no less wise: bringing out the developement of the heart it would make its own ; festering its timid virtues, yielding to its young caprices, training its tendril fancies, losing gradually all separate identity in their clustering foliage; till at length the patron stern and the encircling parasite become us one, nourished by the same sap, and mutually supporting and embellishing each other in undivided sympathy. Such is the progress

of a successful passion between beings of unequal ages, but of similar natures, undefaced by violent disputes, and those odious reconciliations, every one of which steal something from lover's original stock. And if failure meets the man of mature age who ventures on the conquest of young beauty, it comes | ruary 1836. without disgrace, for he rarely hazards by a too rapid advance the chance of too violent a check. He looks out for symptous, and is not so blinded but that he can perceive the breakers wnich warn him of the rock. Hence, when he fails, his rising is not turned to lasting hatred. No ruffian jealousy tramples out the memory of hope ; nor is wounded pride left festering into fierce revenge. He can make allowance for her who was worthy of his affection ; and he can admire and esteem even when he may not dare to love her.

Politeness. þÿ No station, rank, or talents, can ever excuse a man for neglecting the civilities due from man to man. When Clement XIV. ascended the papal chair, the Ambassadors of the several states represented at his Court waited on his holiness with their congratulations. As they were introduced, and severally bowed, he also bowed, to return the compliment. On this the master of the ceremonies told his holiness that he should not have returned their salute. ' O, I beg your pardon,' said he ; '1 have not been Pope long enough to forget good manners.'

All went on pretty well until midnight ; when George Frederick getting very drunk, his host began to be tired of his company. George took the hint, and his host lighted him down stairs into the hall ; when Cooke, laying hold of both his ears, shouted, " Have 1, George Frederick Cooke, degraded myself by dining with brick-layers to meet box-keepers ?" tripped up his heels, and left him sprawling in darkness. " A wise son maketh a Glad Mother ." A wise mother, and her wiser son, were sitting before a roaring fire one cold and dreary evening, when a brand suddenly fell, and scattered the coals in every direction, one of which got into a crack in the floor, and soon set the boards in a blaze. The old lady seized the tea kettle from the corner, and was about applying its boiling contents to the extinguishment of the flames, when the hopeful youth cried out, " Why mother, you fool you, don't you know that hot water wouldn't put out fire ?" She stayed her hand upon hearing this important fact, and before she could procure any cold water, none being at hand, the fire had become unmanageable, and the house was burnt down.

Breach of promise. þÿ An amusing, and rather interesting case, for the breach of a marriage promise, was tried last week, at the Renselaer Circuit Court, before Judge Vanderpoel. The plaintiff, lluldah Smalley, was of a " certain age" which as Byron has it, " is most uncertain age," in truth she is a such a personage as a late monarch would have toasted, had he been blessed with a sight ol her multitudimous attractions. She was a capital pie and pudding maker? cooked to turn, a was a first rate manager for an old bachelor, or mourning widower, and to sum up, she was þÿ unmarried. The defendant, Mr. Eli Uouglass, is a man of years, and experience þÿ sixty and six summers, have passed over his head, and he is now a hearty widower, with a young heart and warm feelings, but a " frosty pow." The days alolted by law, for mourning his third and last time at the Premises; þÿ deceased better half, had long since expired. He had some half dozen pledges of conubial bliss, to provide for, and bring up in the right path, and he a lone man, deemed that he was scarcely capable of undertaking the dangerous task. He wanted a house keeper, a manager, a sort of lynx eyed Duenna, who, while she had charge of his household, could whip the girls, and shut the boys up for any misdemeanor. He cast his eyes on Huldah, or rather Huldah cast her eyes on the situation þÿ she obtained it, and for some time things went prosperously on. Leap year at length came around. Leap year, that blessing to modest bachelois, and

marrying widowers. Uumor with her hundred thousand tongues, had dared to send abroad hints that Huldah, being unmariied, ought not to live in the same house with such a hearty old gentleman. The old women shook their wise heads. The young ones tittered as they talked it over, and the godly Deacons turned aside their pious eyes, and turned up their Christian noses as they passed the house of the devoted Eli. Some oh! crones, whispered into the ears of the too credulous Huldah, the ominous words " leap year," and told her of its privileges, its blessings and its rewards þÿ she was a woman of nerve þÿ she wanted a husband, and a hus. band she would have, and where could she find a better one that Eli, " Uncle Eli," as she affectionately called him. She saw him one day in the garden, alone, and working. Like a second Eve she went forth to tempt him The apple was herself, she offered it. " 1 don't know" quietly said Uncle Eli, leaning over the top of his rake as Adam did over a branch of the Tree of Knowledge. Now Huldah was not a passionate lady, but to have such an insult put upon her, was

more than human nature could withstand þÿ She thought by day, and she dreamed by night, of water, steel, or poison-ranything to compass her revenge. At length she came across the path of one of those things vulgarly called " Land Sharks," but modernized into " Lawyers." She told him of her distress, of her sufferings, of her desire of revenge. She þÿthreatened Madam," " said he, " try something more potent than water, steel or poi- ' " þÿson" try the L- a w. She blessed him as her preserving angel, she thanked him, she feed him. " Uncle Eli" was sued for a " breach of marriage promiss," and after a patient hearing of all the testimony, pro and con, Judge Vanderpoel charged the jury, that although " Uncle Eli" could not be held by law to marry the fair spinster, yet by all the laws of honor and gallantry, he was bound to marry any lady who offered herself on the leap year. The jury being composed mostly of married men, and widowers, very ungallantly returned a verdict for the defendant, and Huldah Was left to mourn, and try another, and a better plan.

Boot Blacking. þÿ Warren the Boot Blacking manufacturer in London, has a retired residence ten miles from the city, keeps his carriage, goes in it to London in the morning, puts on liis apron, arid works all day in his shop, and returns in his carriage at evening. He employs a poet who does nothing else but to vary his metre and modes of illustration in singing the praises of Warren's Blacking. It is not at all surprising that Warren has realised an immense sum in the sale of this article, for there is not a newspaper or periodical in all Great Britain or Ireland, which he has not patronized in the way of advertising. In fact his advertisement appears in almost every part of Europe, and he has agents in every principal town. It is stated that 1,300,600 dollars are annually expended in London for advertising this single article of blacking !

By recent arrivals from New York advices to 9th May are received : þÿ The war in Texas assumes a serious and sanguinary character ; Santa Anna commands in person the invading army ; no quarter is given ; the garrison of Goliad are said to have shared the fate of that of St. Antonio L)e Bexar, the army of Santa Anna is 5,000 strong, principally cavalry ; the women and children in Texas were abandoning their homes, and taking passage for the United States. Gen. Houston, was awaiting the Mexican army, approaching him on the Colorado. Dr. Harrison, son of General Harrison now a candidate for the Presidency of the U. S. was killed in cold blood by the Mexicans, St. Anna had issued a proclamation giving freedom to all Slaves in Texas, agreeably to Mexican laws. Gen. Gaines of the U. S. army had been ordered on to the Texian Frontier, to protect the interests of the U. S., he had written to Santa Anna to know if he had authorized the Camanches and other Indian tribes to commit acts of hostility against the whites. Much alarm existed in Louisiana for fear of Indian incursions, and consequent insurrection among the Negroes; the congress of the U. S. had authorized the raising of additional regiments of Cavalry, or mounted riflemen, to protect the Southern Frontier. A large meeting was held in New York, Col. Swartout presiding, and resolutions to support the Texians in their struggle for Independence, were passed ; 100,000 Dollars was subscribed for this purpose. The Indians in Florida have retreated to
their Swamps and Impenitrable morasses; Gen. Scott found it impossible to bring them to action. Thirty five millions of Dollars were on hand in the U. >S. Treasury the 1st of May.

West Indian Silk. þÿ Considerable interest was excited on the Royal Exchange on Saturday by the production of the first sample of raw silk ever raised in Guadeloupe, the filature of which was exceedingly fine and the coucons larger than those produced either in Italy, or India. The attention of the West India planters has been much directed to the possibility of the cultivation of silk on our West India Colonics, as the new system of labor, and the probable repeal of the imposts on East India Sugar, will make the production of this latter far less profitable than it has hitherto been. The rearing of the silk worm in those colonies will therefore very likely be early determined on by the colonists, and certainly from the specimen produced, those who may enter into this new speculation are justified in being most sanguine of success.

Definition of a Gentleman. þÿ Gentility is neither in birth, manner, nor fashion þÿ but in the mind þÿ A high sense of honour þÿ a determination never to take a mean advantage of another þÿ an adherence to truth, delicacy, and politeness towards those with whom you may have dealings þÿ are the essential and distinguishing characteristics of a gentleman. From Hints on Etiquette.

Spitting of Blood. þÿ Cases not (infrequently occur in which much unnecessary alarm is created by the issue of blood from the mouth, which is supposed to proceed from the lungs or the stomach, but which, on examination, is found to have its source in the fauces, posterior nares, or gums. A case of this kind is related in a late number of the Dublin Journal. The individual, a delicate lady awoke at 5 o'clock in the morning, with what she culled a ' spitting of blood.' The remedies resorted to were without avail, until the arrival of the second physician, who, on examining the mouth, discovered that the haemorrhage issued from the sockets of two of the lower incisor teeth, which were loose. The bleeding was easily arrested, after extracting the teeth. þÿ Boston Medical Journal.
